newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Negotiators upbeat as S.Africa-EU trade talks start.
newsitem.headline: Negotiators upbeat as S.Africa-EU trade talks start.

text.p: South Africa and the European Union started two days of tough negotiations on Friday to iron out deep-seated differences over a planned trade and development deal.
Both sides said they were committed to reaching agreement on a package which could reap rich rewards for their export industries.
"We hope that the negotiations will be very constructive and see the establishment of cordial relations," said South Africa's ambassador to the EU and head of delegation, Eltie Links.

Asked if the EU was optimistic, Ian Fletcher, multilateral trade expert at the European Commission, told reporters: "That is certainly the case. We are here with a full team and that speaks for itself."
But negotiators said this weekend's talks would probably only be a precursor to further, more detailed negotiations.
"We see it as laying the basic principles of both sides for them to launch their respective positions," Links said.

The EU first set out its terms for a free trade deal in March, but Pretoria says that proposal does not go far enough in recognising South Africa's development needs and those of the wider southern Africa region.

The EU has offered post-apartheid South Africa only partial membership of the Lome Convention, which grants favourable access to EU markets to developing countries elsewhere in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific.
Brussels argues relatively developed South Africa cannot expect the same generous terms as the poorest African states.
It calculates 96 percent of South Africa's exports would still enter the EU duty-free.

But plans to exclude 39 percent of farm exports, in order to protect European farmers, have angered Pretoria. It is demanding the EU open up a far greater percentage of its markets to South African exporters than it in turn should open to the EU.
Pretoria also wants development assistance to help the economy to adjust to further trade liberalisation.

Another sticking point is compensation for South Africa's neighbours Botswana, Namibia, Lesotho and Swaziland in the Southern African Customs Union who stand to lose valuable customs levies under a free trade deal.

South African officials this week called on the EU to rethink its approach, to ensure any accord was a wider package to promote development in the region, rather than just a reciprocal deal to cut industrial and agricultural tariffs.
The prize for both sides is great, in both political and economic terms.
For South Africa a deal on the right terms would be a major economic fillip, according to Dave Mohr, chief economist at life assurance giant Old Mutual in Cape Town.
"Access to a huge market like Europe on favourable terms will be a major plus for South Africa," he said.
Some 40 percent of South Africa's exports go to EU member states and more than one third of its exports are of EU origin.
